newsitem.title: NIGERIA: U.S. says Nigeria hasn't asked to question envoy.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says Nigeria hasn't asked to question envoy.

text.p: The United States embassy in Nigeria on Wednesday said it had not received a request to interrogate the ambassador about terrorist bombings after the police chief said he would need permission to do so.

"In response to Inspector General (Ibrahim) Coomassie's statement ... that he would require a diplomatic immunity waiver to interrogate Ambassador (Walter) Carrington and other U.S. Embassy staff...the American embassy in Lagos notes that it has never received such a request," an embassy statement said.

In a speech on Tuesday Nigeria's police chief said he would require Carrington's diplomatic immunity to be waived to question him about a spate of bombings blamed on opponents of military ruler General Sani Abacha.
"We certainly require diplomatic immunity waiver to allow us to interrogate the U.S. ambassador and several staff of the embassy," Coomassie said.

Politically-volatile Nigeria has been hit by a series of blasts since December, most of which have targeted military vehicles. The most recent, in May, killed five worshippers at a mosque in the eastern city of Onitsha.

U.S. Ambassador Walter Carrington has severely criticised Abacha's government for human rights abuses, especially the holding of political prisoners, and its programme to restore democracy by October 1998.
Coomassie said he hoped the United States, as well as Britain and Spain, would allow the Nigerian police to conduct investigations and possibly extradition proceedings in the three countries.

Political analysts say relations between Nigeria and its former friends in the West are at the lowest point since the hanging of author Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other activists triggered international outrage in 1995.
